short.title: DUBOIS VS WARDLEY II — THE FIRST 60 SECONDS
short.voiceoverScript: Wardley put Dubois down twice, but Dubois came back to stop him. Here's what actually matters in the rematch. Wardley must pressure without standing in the line of fire. Dubois needs the jab and his exits early, not just the big right hand. Who's making the better adjustment? The full breakdown is on Aura Fight Club.

youtube.title: Dubois vs Wardley II: What must change in the rematch?
youtube.voiceoverScript:
Two knockdowns in the first fight. An eleventh-round stoppage. And now, five months later, Dubois and Wardley are running it back.

Everybody knows these two heavyweights can hurt each other. But I think the rematch will be decided by something far less spectacular: what happens in the seconds after a punch lands.

Let's go back to Manchester in May. Wardley put Dubois down almost immediately, then dropped him again in round three. If you only watch those highlights, you might think Wardley had the number of his opponent. But Dubois regrouped, began imposing himself and eventually stopped Wardley in round eleven to take the WBO heavyweight title.

That gives us an unusual rematch. The man who lost already knows he can hurt the champion. And the champion knows that even a disastrous start doesn't necessarily mean the fight is lost.

The first adjustment I want to see is Dubois's jab. He shouldn't be using it just to touch his opponent and tick a box for the judges. He needs the jab to control where Wardley puts his feet. When Wardley has to reset his stance, Dubois can work behind a much safer right hand.

But there is an important detail here. A jab is only useful if the boxer is defensively responsible after throwing it. Dubois cannot plant his feet, reach with the lead hand and leave himself directly in Wardley's power lane. Wardley has already shown he can interrupt Dubois's combinations with a dangerous overhand right.

So for Dubois, I would be watching for a double jab, a compact right hand, and then a small angle out. Not a huge, dramatic movement. Just enough to make Wardley change his feet before the next exchange.

Now let's look at Wardley. His problem isn't that he can't hurt Dubois. We saw him do that twice. The question is whether he can protect the success he creates.

In the first meeting, the knockdowns were not enough to stop Dubois from working his way back into the fight. That tells me Wardley needs a different plan once he has landed his best shot. He can't stay in front of Dubois to admire it. He needs a half-step off line, a return to his guard and another entry from a different angle.

Picture it on a ring diagram. Wardley moves forward, tries to catch Dubois during an exchange, and then exits across the edge of the champion's lead foot instead of retreating straight back. That forces Dubois to find him again, rather than automatically following up with his heavier punches.

Of course, there is a trade-off. If Wardley becomes too cautious or spends the entire fight moving away, he may lose the aggressive unpredictability that makes him dangerous. That's why I don't want him simply turning into an outside boxer. He needs controlled pressure. Short bursts, quick exits and another entry before Dubois can settle.

The middle rounds could be especially important. Think about rounds four through eight. This is where the first fight gradually stopped being about Wardley's explosive early success and became a test of repeatable offence and defence. Dubois's work accumulated. The physical cost to Wardley kept rising.

This time, Wardley needs to stop that pattern developing. He needs to be able to win individual exchanges and then recover his defensive position. A fighter can land the cleaner shot and still lose the wider tactical battle if every exchange leaves him in range for the heavier response.

There is also an interesting psychological element. Dubois has talked about his preparation for the first encounter. Wardley has questioned that explanation. We can't verify every detail of either training camp from outside, and I don't think those comments should decide our prediction.

What we can verify is what happened inside the ropes: Dubois was dropped twice and came back to finish the fight. Wardley was dangerous enough to put him in trouble. Both fighters now know exactly what the other man can do.

Here's what I'll be looking for in the first three rounds on Saturday. Does Dubois establish that jab and finish combinations with his guard and balance intact? And after Wardley throws his overhand right, does he change the angle or does he linger in front of Dubois?

If Dubois keeps collecting those predictable exchanges and turning them into sustained pressure, he should become stronger as the fight wears on. But if Wardley keeps making Dubois miss after landing, the fight could look very different from May.

My prediction is Daniel Dubois by a late stoppage, somewhere from rounds eight to eleven. That's the pick on the AURA Fight Club website as well.

But there's a genuine upset case for Wardley. He's already proved he can create an early crisis. If he combines that threat with more disciplined defensive positioning afterwards, this isn't just the same fight playing out again.

That's the difference between being a dangerous puncher and becoming a complete heavyweight. It isn't just about who can land the big right hand. It's who can control the next moment.

So what do you think? Will Dubois's jab and sustained work take over again? Or can Wardley make the one adjustment that changes the whole heavyweight picture?
